newsitem.title: UK: Mark slumps to fresh lows in late Europe.
newsitem.headline: Mark slumps to fresh lows in late Europe.

text.p: The mark slid against its crosses in late European trade as the German draft budget, officially unveiled on Friday, heightened perceptions that European monetary union will result in a soft euro currency.
Mark cross sentiment was also dampened because the mark was bruised across the board, dropping to its lowest against the dollar in nearly six years and its weakest against sterling since April 1991.
Bonn's draft supplementary budget for 1997 showed the projected deficit for this year would increase to 71.2 billion marks from the originally planned 53.3 billion.

However, German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said Germany would still be able to fulfill the Maastricht criterion target of a budget deficit that was 3.0 percent of GDP this year. EMU candidate nations will be judged whether they fill the necessary economic criteria on the basis of their 1997 data.
The mark was sold off, with the market greeting with scepticism Waigel's reassurance that Germany will still meet the target required for the single currency.

"People are pretty doubtful. It's been obvious for some time that Germany won't make 3.0 percent, and that even if they did, it would be through some sleight of hand," said Itsuro Karasawa, assistant general manager at Sakura Bank in London. "As a result, the mark became a sell."

The German budget news led to perceptions that EMU will be pushed forward but with a soft euro currency since few, if any, of the members were now likely to meet the criteria, traders and analysts said.
The mark had slipped to 3.3768/73 French francs by 1415 GMT after rising to a one-month high of 3.3823 in early European trade. It was at 3.3796/01 in late trade on Thursday.
Against the lira, it was at a five-month low of 971.10/40 against late Thursday's 976.60/80.

Traders also pointed out that the mark's fall today was all the sharper because it had been bought back amid a corrective rise on Thursday, adding that yesterday's rise had not been a change in mark sentiment.

Since information on the budget had been leaked in recent days, the market had been fully expecting a higher budget deficit, and that Germany would insist it would make the three-percent goal somehow in spite of this.

However, the market would have been more sanguine about the situation if the government had shown some concern about the burgeoning deficit and shown it was making efforts to remedy the situation, analysts said.

"Waigel is still operating on the assumption that the increase in the deficit... would be counterbalanced by the better numbers they get from the local states. But the local states are facing the same (budgetary) problems Waigel is facing," said Hans-Guenter Redeker, senior economist at Chase Investment Bank here.

"So the market is obviously thinking the higher deficit numbers mean we are talking about a broader and softer EMU, and this is reflected in the market's activity where people are selling the core European currencies against the dollar," Redeker said.
Such sentiment was also causing a flight out of marks into sterling, seen as a safe haven with its position outside the EMU bloc and its attractively higher interest rates, said Sakura's Karasawa.
Sterling/mark had stormed up to reach just above the key 3.00 mark level today, although it had receded slightly to 2.9966/76 by late European trade.
Elsewhere in Europe, moves in the Portuguese escudo were choppy as the Bank of Portugal made a surprise move to cut all three of its official market rates by 30 basis points.
The repo rate was cut to 5.7 percent, the drain rate to 5.4 percent and the emergency lending rate to 7.4.
Mark/escudo was at its session low of 100.80/85 in late trade, compared with 100.96/99 on Thursday.
-- Chizu Nomiyama, London Forex Desk, +44-171-542-6721
